source_text: Deinde quia multa in propositionibus invenitur diversitas, dixeras: Non esse sine voluntate delictum, et respondisti: sed per unius voluntatem esse delictum. Numquid concinit superiori definitioni, quae ablativi casus praepositione munitur, secuta responsio per praepositionem accusativi casus illata? Quaesitum erat utrum esset crimen sine voluntate, quod non posse constiterat; tu subdidisti per unum hominem intrasse peccatum, cum non referret per quid coepisset, sed sine quo esse non posset.
pass_a_gloss: Then because much diversity is found in propositions, you had said: There is not offense without will, and you replied: but through the will of one there is offense. Does the following reply, brought in through a preposition of the accusative case, agree with the earlier definition, which is fortified by a preposition of the ablative case? It had been asked whether there was a charge without will, which had stood as not able to be; you subjoined that through one man sin entered, when it did not matter through what it had begun, but without which it could not be.

lemmas.lexica: LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin

pass_b_english: Again, there is a large difference between the propositions. You said, “There is no offense without will,” and answered, “But there is an offense through one person’s will.” Does the following reply, introduced by a preposition taking the accusative case, agree with the earlier definition, secured by a preposition taking the ablative case? The question was whether a crime could exist without will, and it had been established that it could not. You added that sin entered through one man. Yet the issue was not through what it began, but without what it could not exist.

choices.why: Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
Julian's forensic/moral fault tied to will, not a substance in nature.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
